label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
Yep Mikaela, we went onto 10 in 7 on 21 Sept, after mating had started. We’ve got 290 cows, mostly 3-way crossbreds. We skip Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday arvos, plus Sunday arvo, so four once-a-day milkings a week. Morning milking is still 5.15 every day.

The honest production answer is that milksolids are down about 6% on the same weeks last year, going off the Fonterra app. Our rep had told us to expect an 8-10% hit, so it’s been better than that here so far. It’s not a whole-season result yet though, and it’s not a tidy trial either. I wouldn’t take my 6% and bank on getting exactly that at yours, especially starting after Christmas rather than when we did. Also, 6% is still 6% — it isn’t free.

The cells did jump. We went from around 110,000 to roughly 180,000 in the first three weeks, and we’re back around 135,000 now. So they didn’t stay mental, but it wasn’t nothing either.

And the worst bit: we had a heifer with mastitis go bad on a skipped arvo. We didn’t spot it until the next morning and she lost a quarter. That’s the part I’d want to know if I was asking somebody else, because you can talk about rosters and percentages and skim over the stuff that actually went wrong. You have to be really on your game with teat spraying and checking the cows on the skip days. If you just drop the arvo and don’t properly look them over, it can bite you.

On the good side, lameness is miles better. We’ve got four on the lame list now compared with 11 this time last year, and our long walk to the back paddocks is 1.8km, so taking those trips out has made a real difference. The cows themselves came round quicker than I expected — about four days of standing at the gate bellowing, then they seemed to work it out and get on with it.

The people side has been just as big. The first skipped Sunday arvo, Dave and I went to Hamilton to see the grandkids. First Sunday off in spring in 20-odd years, which is a bit embarrassing to admit but there you go. Kieran, our 2IC, said it’s the first spring he hasn’t wanted to quit by October. That probably tells you as much about the hours as any number I can give you. And if Tom’s knees are stuffed, I think the arvos off will help him more than anything.

For us, honestly, I wouldn’t go back. The hours alone are worth the 6%. But I’m not going to tell you that automatically makes it right for your place. There’s a real trade-off, and the mastitis risk is real if the checking slips. You’ve also got to decide whether the milk you give up is worth what you get back in sounder cows, better knees and staff who aren’t looking for the gate themselves.

If you’re at the field day on the 19th, come and find me and we can go through the shed rosters and the actual numbers, including the rough bits. Or ring me if you want — much easier than me trying to text it all with these thumbs.
